To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

LN isoforms 8, 10, and 10-containing protein complexes are the primary constituents of the subendo-thelial basement membrane favor-ing interaction with extravasating neoplastically transformed lymphocytes.
the LN-8 and -10 isoforms are the primary components of the vascular basement membrane promoting interaction of neoplastic cells with endothelial cells.

the interaction of neoplastic cells with the subendothelium of the blood vessel wall is promoted by the expression of a number of laminin isoforms, which are differentially expressed in the vascular structures of the human organism and which, in turn, are differentially recognized by the neoplastic lymphocyte population.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the characterization of the molecular basis of the interaction of LN isoforms with neoplastic B cells and the identification of the LN isoform(s) that may play a role in the extravasated of neoplastic T lymphocytes.

the characterization of the molecular basis of LN-mediated cell interactions and may provide the basis for a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms of LN-dependent neoplastic lymphocyte extravasation and may have important therapeutic implications.
the identification of LN isoforms and LN complexes that may be involved in neoplastic lymphocyte extravasation and the definition of their molecular mechanisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the subendothelium of the human vascular tree contains a number of LNs that can potentially promote adhesion of neoplastic cells and that the engagement of these LNs by the transformed lymphocytes may be a prerequisite for the extravasation process.
LN-8, LN-10, LN-1, and LN-2 may play a role in the extravasating of neoplastic cells in the human vascular compartment.

LNs may play a role in the extravasating of neoplastic cells, and that the ability of LN isoforms to promote adhesion to lymphocytes may be the result of the differential expression of LN receptors in different neoplastic cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the subendothelium of the vascular compartment is composed of different LN isoforms that, in turn, are differentially recognized by lymphocytes, thus providing the molecular basis for a mechanism that could be exploited in the treatment of neoplastic diseases.
the LN isoforms are not only a structural component of the subendothedial basement membrane, but they may also play an important role in the regulation of neoplastic cell extravasation.

the LN isoform composition of the subendotheial basement membrane may be a key determinant of the interaction of neoplastic cells with the endothelium and that the LN isoforms 8, 10, and 10-containing protein complexes may be the primary determinants of the adhesion of extravasating lymphocytes to the vascular basement membrane.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the subendothelium of vascular structures may be the primary site of interaction of extravasated lymphocytes with LMs.

LN-8, LN-10, or LN-10-containing complexes may be implicated in lymphocyte homing and that the interaction of LN-8 and/or LN-10 with neoplastic B and/or T cells may be involved in the extravasational process of lymphoma and leukemia.

the use of LN-specific antibodies may provide a valuable diagnostic tool for the detection of neoplastic cells at the site of extravasation, and that the use of purified LNs may provide a valuable source of antigens for the development of novel immunotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of lymphoid neoplasms.
